newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN meeting ends on uncertain note over Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN meeting ends on uncertain note over Cambodia.

text.p: A meeting of Southeast Asian nations ended on a note of uncertainty over Cambodia on Friday as foreign ministers said they needed to confirm Phnom Penh's position on mediation before resuming efforts to bring about peace.

After receiving conflicting signals from Cambodia's leaders, the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) said in a closing communique it would send three ministers "to assist Cambodia to find a peaceful resolution of the situation in that country".

Cambodia this week was to have joined ASEAN along with Burma and Laos. But ASEAN decided to postpone its admission indefinitely after Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's bloody putsch against First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh early in July.
The ceremony ending the two-day annual ASEAN meeting was delayed for two hours as they tried to understand Phnom Penh's position toward their offers to mediate in the crisis.
Last weekend, Hun Sen told a delegation of three ASEAN foreign ministers that the group had no role at all to play in settling Cambodia's troubles.
That position seemed reversed abruptly on Wednesday, when Cambodia's emissary to the talks Foreign Minister Ung Huot said Phnom Penh had decided it wanted ASEAN to act as mediator.

Hun Sen on Thursday said ASEAN had a role in ensuring Cambodia's stability but on Friday said he had meant that role should be to prevent "foreign interference into the internal affairs of Cambodia" and that the country's problems should be resolved internally.

Southeast Asian foreign ministers also "expressed serious concerns over well coordinated efforts to destabilise ASEAN currencies for self-serving purposes, thus threatening the stability of all ASEAN economies".

Almost every country in ASEAN -- which now groups Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Brunei, Laos and Burma -- has seen its currency weakened by marauding traders in recent weeks.

Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad introduced the theme in his keynote address on Thursday, condemning "rogue speculators" and "anarchists" who wanted weaker economies "to submit to the dictatorship of international manipulators".
Malaysian Foreign Minister Adbullah Ahmad Badawi, chairman of the meeting, said the foreign ministers did not suggest any new measures to deal with the problem.
He said they wanted central banks and finance ministers in the region "to intensify coordination".
"If we can do it together it would be better... because there is a very strong link among members of ASEAN," he said.
Abdullah also defended ASEAN's policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma, saying Rangoon's military rulers have promised constitutional reform leading to elections.
Burma's generals cancelled the results of 1990 elections won by Nobel peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy. Talks on constitutional reform have dragged on for years.
Abdullah said ASEAN was prepared to defend the policy at the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) on Sunday.

Asia's premier vehicle for political and security talks, ARF brings the 10 southeast Asian countries together with 11 Asian and Western powers, including the United States and the European Union, Burma's biggest critics.
Economic and trade issues are likely to dominate the ARF meeting, along with Cambodia and Burma, diplomats said.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright said in a speech in Los Angeles this week she would press for better enforcement of intellectual property rights, greater transparency in government contracts and higher standards against bribery and corruption.
She is also expected to ask for ASEAN's help in reaching a global agreement on liberalising financial services.
ASEAN, for its part, is expected to object to western governments linking human rights with trade privileges.

The ARF meeting is also expected to talk about disarmament issues, tensions over conflicting claims in the South China Sea, stability on the Korean peninsula and freedom of navigation in the South Pacific sea lanes.
